# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common belief, deeply embedded in how most organizations operate, that a successful meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. The goal, we assume, is alignment: a room full of people who have converged on the same answer, ready to move forward in lockstep. Managers often measure their own effectiveness by their ability to manufacture this kind of harmony. When a meeting ends with unanimous agreement, we feel we've accomplished something.

But this intuition deserves scrutiny. Agreement, it turns out, is not always a sign that a problem has been solved. Sometimes it's a sign that a problem has been papered over. Sometimes everyone in the room is wrong in the same direction, and the shared confidence that comes from agreement makes the eventual correction more painful. Sometimes people agree out loud while privately harboring doubts they never voice—doubts that would have been valuable to surface while there was still time to act on them.
